recordings.type: adult, call, life stage uncertain, sex uncertain
recordings.rmk:
These swifts were recorded as they flew over a neighborhood in the evening. The area was primarily covered in houses, streets, and ornamental plants, though it is near a few more varied habitats. To the southwest is a reed- and willow-filled marsh in an abandoned quarry, whereas meadows variably populated by grasses and occasional shrubs like coyote brush are found to the north. A nearby forest is largely made up of a variety of evergreen trees such as coast live oak, coast redwood, and Douglas-fir. 

My recording was made at dusk in clear weather. The light was decent, but fading rather quickly. The swifts were acrobatically swooping overhead, presumably either interacting with one another in some way or chasing aerial prey. 

I modified this recording extensively, using Audacity to reduce noise, increase volume, and cut out excess non-swift sounds.

recordings.loc: Baton Rouge, East B. R. Parish, LA
recordings.rmk: The chipping rattle was given at the bottom of a shallow U shuttle display by a bird seen naked eye (orange-colored gorget seen). I actually thought it might be a Selasphorus at the time (although I'd already seen a male Archilochus that morning), but the display differed from the one the Selasphorus was performing, and was more shallow. I couldn't see the bird the display was directed toward. Comparing to a few recordings of shuttle display in A. colubris, this recording sounds most like that, so I am identifying the cut as that species.

recordings.loc: Skidaway Island, Chatham County, GA USA
recordings.rmk: A compilation of 4 recordings over two days  to adequately capture the vocalizations as well as the sound of the wing-beat.  The recordings have all been significantly shortened since the birds visits and vocalizing were entirely random.  Other than that the gain has been balanced to -9 for all and noise reduction was used on three.  The vocalizations occurred usually by the dominant bird at the feeding cluster when another bird approached.  However at times a short utterance could be heard when no other bird was apparent.

recordings.loc: Alva, Lee County, Florida
recordings.rmk:
This recording was taken from an oxbow on the Caloosahatchee River at about 10:30 pm, March 11. I know it's a limpkin in the foreground but there's another bird you can hear distinctly.

I haven't heard this sound coming from any of the limpkin recordings that I've listened to. I suspect that it may be another limpkin occasionally coming in to roost. Some of my birding friends have suggested that it may be a frog but the night this recording was taken we heard the bird come in from upstream and land near the limpkin.

Please chime in If you have heard a limpkin or another bird making this noise.

Thanks in advance, 

Paul

recordings.loc: Portage Point  (near  Escanaba), Delta County, Michigan
recordings.rmk: Unmodified recording.  This morning 35 degrees with a wintry mix of snow and sleet. Pair of Greater Yellowlegs feeding in water just offshore of the beach at Portage Point. When I saw them, I tried to remain out of sight behind a shrub near them, but they saw me and took off, calling in flight. The bird that was flying in front was the one that made the first call. I am not sure which bird made the second call.

Neah Bay, Clallam County, Washington
recordings.rmk: Song(?) given by adult bird among the cliffs toward the end of Cape Flattery Trail, Neah Bay, Washington, USA, where they appear to have a large breeding population. The wind and waves were both high during recording, so a High Pass Filter was used in a desperate attempt to cut back on noise, and the bird's sounds were very slightly amplified. The bird appeared to give the song right before taking off from the cliffs and heading out to sea, or in flight low over the ocean on their way back into the cliffs. Weather was cool and windy, with thinning mist preventing clear views of ocean horizon, along with overcast skies.

Wilder Ranch SP, Santa Cruz County, California
recordings.type: call, life stage uncertain, sex uncertain
recordings.rmk: Several groups of Pigeon Guillemot were nesting along the sides of Fern Grotto Beach, and they seemed to take little notice of me as I was recording them and standing nearby. There was some vegetation on the cliffsides, and leading up to the beach, but apart from some dried-up plant matter, none was near the crags I saw the birds nesting in. All birds I saw were adults, but juveniles may have been more hidden from view. The weather was cloudy, with temperatures being in the cooler range. As usual, I boosted this recording's volume on Audacity but did little else to it.
